claims.claim: George Daniels worked at Chess Records, then at a Black-owned record wholesale company on Michigan Avenue.
claims.note: HistoryMakers finding aid (EAD A2007_156) states both employments explicitly.

claims.claim: Daniels managed a wholesale record shop in 1968 and assumed ownership in 1969, renaming it George's Music Room.
claims.note: HistoryMakers finding aid gives the 1968 manage / 1969 assume-ownership sequence and the renaming.

claims.claim: George's Music Room became an in-store promotional stop for recording artists.
claims.note: Stated in the HistoryMakers finding aid.

claims.claim: Daniels founded the National United Independent Retailers, an organization dedicated to protecting African American-owned independent retailers; the HistoryMakers finding aid dates the founding to 1990.
claims.note: Founding and mission in the finding aid; founding year 1990 per the detailed finding-aid search result.

claims.claim: HistoryMakers characterizes George's Music Room as benefiting surrounding North Lawndale businesses and as a site where Daniels mentored neighborhood youth.
claims.note: The archive's own characterization; infrastructure interpretation built on it is our analysis, not the archive's wording.

claims.claim: Bob Koester founded Delmark Records in 1953 (originally 'Delmar') and relocated the label to Chicago in 1958.
claims.note: Delmark's own institutional tribute page states founding year, original name, and relocation.

claims.claim: In 1959 Koester took over Seymour's Jazz Mart at 439 S. Wabash Ave. from songwriter Seymour Schwartz and renamed it Jazz Record Mart.
claims.note: Stated on Delmark's institutional page (via quoted Block Club reporting); exact year and address given.

claims.claim: Delmark Records was subsidized by the store's sales, giving Koester freedom to record and curate across genres.
claims.note: Delmark's own page states the subsidy relationship explicitly; the core store-label symbiosis claim.

claims.claim: Jazz Record Mart's final address was 27 E. Illinois St.; the store closed in 2016, with Koester attributing the closure to rising rent.
claims.note: Delmark page quotes the 2016 DNAinfo report with Koester's rent explanation.

claims.claim: Calkins (2019) finds that between 1980 and 1990, record stores outside majority-white areas had significantly higher failure probabilities than stores within majority-white areas.
claims.note: Peer-reviewed article, City & Community 18(3), 853-873, DOI 10.1111/cico.12433; finding stated in abstract and reproduced in the dissertation excerpt.

claims.claim: Calkins (2019) finds record stores were once more clustered in predominantly Black areas than they were by 2010.
claims.note: Stated in the study's findings; strongest quantitative support for unequal infrastructure loss.

claims.claim: Davis (2011) reports that close to 1,000 African American-owned record stores operated in the South during their heyday.
claims.note: Southern Cultures 17(4) article; scale figure is the article's own estimate for the 1960s-70s South.

claims.claim: Davis (2011) documents that Black store owners often had difficulty securing supplier credit and had to pay cash for inventory — a supply-side constraint, not evidence of stores extending credit to customers.
claims.note: Critical distinction preserved: this is wholesale/supplier credit denied to owners, not consumer credit extended by stores.

claims.claim: Vee-Jay Records was founded in 1953 by Vivian Carter and James Bracken, who owned a record store in Gary, Indiana; Carter was also a DJ.
claims.note: Indiana public-history reporting (Indiana Historical Bureau blog / IPM Nightlights). Gary, not Chicago — comparative regional case.

claims.claim: Russell Lee photographed the corner of Maxwell and Halsted Streets, Chicago, in April 1941; the image sits in the Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division, FSA-OWI Collection, reproduction number LC-USF33-012984-M5.
claims.note: Reproduction number from the scholarly figure caption citing LOC P&P; FSA-OWI works carry no known publication restrictions per S05.

claims.claim: George's Music Room stood at 3915 W. Roosevelt Road in North Lawndale.
claims.note: Sibling CTL research (CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 / TRiiBE); not independently verified against city directories in this brief — cap at SUPPORTED.

claims.claim: Imports Etc., on a side street in Chicago's Printers Row, was in 1986 the city's only record store dealing exclusively in dance music; most of its customers were DJs, stocking new 12-inch singles, old Philadelphia soul, and Italian imports.
claims.note: Contemporary SPIN feature (November 1986 issue). The 'only' claim is the reporter's contemporary characterization, not an audited market survey.

claims.claim: After Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk played Telex's 'Brainwash' (Belgian group, English lyrics by Sparks) in his sets, Imports Etc. sold 1,000 copies in two weeks.
claims.note: Participant testimony in contemporary journalism; not audited sales data. Capped at SUPPORTED, not VERIFIED.

claims.claim: Chip E. worked at Imports Etc.; after local DJs played his acetate of 'Like This,' he pressed 1,000 copies (borrowing his mother's income-tax check), sold 500 the first day and the rest within the week.
claims.note: Participant testimony in SPIN 1986 — documents the store-as-label pipeline: DJ-employee -> acetate -> club/radio play -> store sales -> pressing.

claims.claim: The WBMX Hot Mix 5 created record demand before release: DJs brought rough mixes to the show, and exposure ensured enough profit to fund the next pressing.
claims.note: SPIN 1986, quoting participants; J.M. Silk's 'Music Is the Key' reportedly sold 2,000 copies the day it came out after pre-release airplay.

claims.claim: Gramaphone Records opened in 1969.
claims.note: Corroborated across NPR (2021), the Chicago Tribune (2019), and the store's Wikipedia article — multiple strong sources, per red-team rule.

claims.claim: Joe Dale and Carl Borowski took over Gramaphone in 1978, and the store shifted toward dance music in the early 1980s.
claims.note: Joe Dale obituaries (EDM All Day, Electronic Groove, March 2025) corroborate the 1978 takeover and early-1980s dance pivot; specialist press.

claims.claim: Gramaphone employed working DJs — including Derrick Carter, Ralphi Rosario, DJ Sneak, DJ Heather, DJ Colette, Mark Farina, and Jesse De La Peña — functioning as a retail library, peer-learning environment, equipment-advice point, and professional pipeline.
claims.note: Names across NPR, 5 Magazine, Beatsway, Wikipedia; Serafini's equipment-advice role from NPR/BM reporting.

claims.claim: Vivian Carter played records for teenagers in her Gary, Indiana record store, solicited their reactions, and used that feedback in talent and record decisions — a store-as-A&R case.
claims.note: Indiana public-history reporting; comparative case, not a Chicago store.

claims.claim: Before computerized reporting, Billboard's charts drew separately on self-reported record-store sales, DJ playlists, and jukebox plays.
claims.note: Public Radio East history of the Hot 100 methodology; national context — no Chicago-specific reporting-panel source located.

claims.claim: More than 20 Black-owned stores formed the F.A.M.S. Coalition (Forever a Music Store) in 2021, seeking industry support, exclusives, vinyl variants, release parties, and equal opportunity.
claims.note: Radio X (2023) reporting; Drew Mitchell of Chicago's 606 Records quoted advocating equal opportunity for minority-owned stores.

claims.claim: Warner executive Steve Corbin described Black independent stores as important in breaking records in the early 1990s.
claims.note: Industry-executive testimony in Radio X reporting; modern parallel to Daniels's 1990 organizing.

claims.claim: In the Ticketron/Ticketmaster era, concert tickets were commonly bought at record stores; fans lined up outside record stores for tickets.
claims.note: Pollstar (2007) and TicketNews confirm the general US practice; no Chicago-specific store identified as a ticket outlet — that gap is UNRESOLVED (C72).

claims.claim: Ora Nelle (Maxwell Radio) sold discs from a Maxwell Street storefront.
claims.note: Sibling CTL research (CTL-DR-BMI-002 track D); illustrates storefront-as-distribution in the Maxwell Street corridor.

claims.claim: Jukebox operators tracked plays by location and regularly changed selections; Black and working-class artists often reached listeners through jukeboxes despite limited radio access.
claims.note: Smithsonian Magazine history and Absher (2014) monograph, U. Michigan Press. No Chicago store-to-operator link established.

claims.claim: By 1954, Midwest jukebox operators were receiving rising requests for R&B in teenage locations.
claims.note: Absher (2014); adjacent distribution/listening infrastructure, not record stores themselves.

claims.claim: A 1970s Billboard piece documents Black entrepreneurs' barriers in one-stop/wholesale operations, including Jerry Augustus's Hitsville co-op one-stop in New York.
claims.note: Via Indiana University African American Music & Culture Digital Library; national context for Daniels's wholesaling career.

claims.claim: Charles L. Hughes (Country Soul, 2015): country-soul-era record stores sold records but also other goods; staff listened to customer requests; stores were sites of 'musical cross-pollination.'
claims.note: UNC Press blog interview with the scholar; regional (Southern) context, used comparatively.

claims.claim: Gramaphone Records is located at 2843 N. Clark St.; Hyde Park Records at 1377 E. 53rd St.
claims.note: Third Coast Review vinyl-shop directory; secondary directory source.

claims.claim: Joe Dale died in March 2025 (announced March 26, 2025); Gramaphone's statement called him an 'unsung hero of house music.'
claims.note: Two obituaries (EDM All Day, Electronic Groove); the 'unsung hero' phrase is the store's own attributed characterization.

claims.claim: In the Sway's Universe interview, George Daniels describes how labels' distribution and pricing practices undercut Black-owned mom-and-pop stores.
claims.note: Video title and description text verified 2026-09-28; segment-level transcript timestamps still to be logged at publication. Used as illustration of the label-retail conflict claim.

claims.claim: Gramaphone Records was featured in the documentary Better Living Through Circuitry.
claims.note: Wikipedia article claim; fine as corroboration, not sole basis for any infrastructure argument.

claims.claim: Gramaphone was 'the first of its kind in the Chicago area, focusing on vinyl for DJs.'
claims.note: 'First' claims are inherently fragile; this is reported contemporary characterization, used with attribution, not as an audited market fact.

claims.claim: Koester ran Jazz Record Mart for nearly 50 years at multiple Chicago locations before opening Bob's Blues & Jazz Mart in Irving Park in 2016; he sold Delmark to Julia A. Miller in 2018.
claims.note: Delmark page and Block Club obituary; the 2018 sale confirms the label's continuation beyond the store.

claims.claim: George's Music Room's closure date: TRiiBE/sibling reporting says 2010; an IMDb documentary description says 2017.
claims.note: Two secondary sources conflict; no primary source checked. Do not publish an unqualified closing date.

claims.claim: Imports Etc. owner surname: 'Weisburg' in some accounts, 'Weisberg' in others; store name rendered 'Importes, Etc.' and 'Imports Etc.'
claims.note: Spelling variants across sources; brief standardizes on 'Imports Etc.' (SPIN 1986 contemporary spelling) and flags the variants.

claims.claim: The origin of the name 'house music': store bin labeling is one participant account among several (Knuckles's Warehouse vs. Farley's 'nobody in the city was playing imports' account in SPIN 1986).
claims.note: SPIN 1986 itself carries two competing naming accounts; do not publish a settled story.

claims.claim: A 1979 record pool operated at Imports Etc.
claims.note: Later oral history via sibling research; uncorroborated by contemporary documentation.

claims.claim: DJ Ron Hardy used Imports Etc. as a supply base.
claims.note: Sibling-research oral-history lead; SPIN 1986 (contemporary) does not name Hardy in connection with the store.

claims.claim: Koester's store directly incubated Alligator Records, Living Blues magazine, and Flying Fish Records.
claims.note: Depends on an indirectly reproduced Bruce Iglauer quotation; original Tribune/Sun-Times text not located.

claims.claim: The National United Independent Retailers' activities and membership beyond its 1990 founding.
claims.note: Finding aid establishes founding and mission; scope of activity not detailed in located sources.

claims.claim: Imports Etc.'s opening year, closing year, and exact street address.
claims.note: SPIN 1986 locates it only as 'a side street in Chicago's Printers Row'; city-directory work remains.

claims.claim: Whether named Chicago record stores routinely extended credit, layaway, tabs, or delayed payment to retail customers.
claims.note: No Chicago-specific evidence located. Largest uncertainty in the brief. Supplier-credit evidence (C13) must not be misread as customer-credit evidence.

claims.claim: Which Chicago record stores were on Billboard's pre-computerized chart reporting panel.
claims.note: The national methodology (C25) is SUPPORTED; no Chicago-specific panel membership located.

claims.claim: Which Chicago record stores served as Ticketmaster/Ticketron outlets.
claims.note: General practice SUPPORTED (C28); Chicago-specific identification not found.

claims.claim: Specific Chicago record-store-to-jukebox-operator relationships.
claims.note: Jukebox infrastructure context SUPPORTED (C30-C31); store-operator links not established.

claims.claim: George Daniels's role in protecting African American-owned independent retailers is documented through his founding of the National United Independent Retailers (1990) and his HistoryMakers oral history.
claims.note: Archive + interview corroboration; the Sway interview elaborates the label-practice conflict.

claims.claim: The specific form of artist appearances at George's Music Room (in-store performances vs. signings/photo appearances).
claims.note: The HistoryMakers finding aid establishes the store as an artist promotional stop (C03) but does not detail the form those appearances took.

grade_definitions.DISPUTED: Multiple sources conflict; no resolution found yet.
grade_definitions.PROVISIONAL: Plausible and relevant, but resting on indirect quotation, later oral history, or one weak source; needs corroboration before publication as fact.
grade_definitions.SUPPORTED: Well-attested by reputable journalism or specialist reporting, but dependent on a single secondary account or participant testimony.
grade_definitions.UNRESOLVED: No evidence located; an open research question.
grade_definitions.VERIFIED: Directly established by primary or strong institutional evidence (archive, government, label, artist's own records). Per CTL red-team rule, one ordinary secondary source does not equal VERIFIED; corroboration across two or more strong sources also qualifies.
